processing: Fresh flowers rest thinly to lose surface water, are briefly steamed to stop oxidation, then dried on bamboo screens over several days with an indoor airing in between. The steamed blooms press together into flat, cake-like sheets in the old style.
harvest_season: Late autumn, October into November, on dry sunny days in several passes a few days apart. The first pass of closed buds is sold as tai ju; later open flowers make the everyday grades.
appearance_dry: Pale whitish flowers with yellow centres, whole or pressed in flat sheets.
appearance_wet: Whole white flowers with broad petals and yellow centres, opening in the water.
taste_profile: Honeyed and herbal with a pale floral sweetness, a light pleasant bitterness and a long floral finish.

brewing.notes: Glass shows off the flowers. Add a few blooms to ripe pu-erh for the classic ju pu pairing.

vintage_note: Sold by the autumn harvest of the current year, with new stock arriving after the October and November picking. It is not aged: look for pale, whole, sweet-smelling flowers, since dark or crumbled ones have gone past their best. Grade follows the picking, with bud lots (tai ju) above open flowers.
description:
Hangbaiju is the white tea chrysanthemum grown around Tongxiang, near Hangzhou in Zhejiang. It is the classic Chinese chrysanthemum drink and has long been named in the same breath as Long Jing as a local treasure.

The step that defines it is steaming. Flowers get a quick steam that stops them from darkening, then dry slowly on bamboo screens. Too little steam and they darken, too much and they go flat. Old-style flowers arrive pressed into sheets for that reason. Gongju from Huangshan in Anhui is the main contrast, being oven-dried instead.

The cup is pale and honeyed, with a light bitterness that keeps it from being sugary and a floral finish that lingers. It is forgiving: hot water, a few minutes, refill.

Buy pale, whole flowers that smell sweet. Closed buds, sold as tai ju, are the top of the range; open flowers are the everyday drink and often better value.

For a next step, try a few flowers in ripe pu-erh. The ju pu pairing softens the earthiness and freshens the cup.
history:
Tongxiang has grown this flower for centuries, and it is counted among the Eight Zhejiang Herbs (浙八味), a traditional group of medicinal exports. Exact dates for its beginnings are not well documented.

Today it is a large local crop: Tongxiang has more than 40,000 mu planted and a November harvest that draws news photographers to its white fields.
